name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-2
lead: Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 is a synthetic four-amino-acid peptide (acetyl-Lys-Asp-Val-Tyr) used in anti-aging and skin-firming cosmetics, sold by suppliers under names such as Thymulen 4 [1]. It is described as mimicking thymopoietin, a thymus hormone, and is claimed to counter the age-related decline of thymic factors and to support skin immune defences and epidermal regeneration [1].

Published research is limited. A 2018 cell study found that the peptide changed the stiffness and gene expression of cultured keratinocytes [2], and a 2021 randomized study tested a hair lotion that combined it with creatine and B vitamins [3]. No trial has tested the peptide alone on facial wrinkles or firmness.

paras: Supplier-derived descriptions say the peptide stimulates keratinocytes to produce GM-CSF, which promotes maturation of Langerhans cells and thereby raises skin immune surveillance [1]. Such descriptions are manufacturer claims and have not been independently tested in published trials.

A 2021 open, randomized controlled study in women with acute telogen effluvium evaluated a lotion containing creatine, acetyl tetrapeptide-2 and B vitamins for reducing hair loss [3]. Because the lotion combined several actives, the results cannot be attributed to the peptide alone.
No studies were found of acetyl tetrapeptide-2 as a single ingredient in facial skin.

In immortalized human keratinocytes (HaCaT), atomic force microscopy showed that the peptide raised cell stiffness after 48 hours, most notably at a low concentration, and it increased expression of the COL17A1 gene [2]. This was an in vitro study, not a test on living skin.
The peptide is marketed in serums, creams and masks [1]. No looksmaxxing community discussion was identified.

card.summary: A thymopoietin-mimic cosmetic peptide with cell-culture data and one combination-lotion hair study.
card.note: No trial of the peptide alone; the hair study used a multi-ingredient lotion.

quick.overview:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 is a short cosmetic peptide marketed for firmness and skin regeneration, and also appears in some hair lotions.

Research is thin: a keratinocyte cell study and a randomized study of a lotion that combined it with creatine and B vitamins.
quick.mechanism: Suppliers say it mimics thymopoietin and prompts keratinocytes to release GM-CSF, activating skin Langerhans cells. In cultured cells it raised stiffness and COL17A1 expression.
quick.risks: No safety data were found beyond its status as a cosmetic ingredient; the supporting claims are largely manufacturer-reported.
